chunks.content: Nadodrze is an osiedle (settlement/district) in central Wrocław on the right bank of the Oder, formally delineated in 1991. Its area was incorporated into the city between 1768 and 1808 after the demolition of the city fortifications. Population was 22,259 as of 31 Dec 2024. It is a 19th-century artisan district of decorative historicist tenements, severely damaged in WWII and long considered run-down, now known for its art scene, murals, workshops and cafes.

Plac Św. Macieja (St. Maciej's Square) lies at the heart of Nadodrze and is described as the most inviting and expansive of the district's green squares, a pleasant spot for a rest during a walk through the neighbourhood.

Nadodrze underwent a major urban revitalisation in the 2010s, transforming a previously run-down area into a creative district. The strategy favoured murals and artistic installations over demolition; over 30 street-art works decorate walls and courtyards. Landmarks include the 1868 Nadodrze railway station, a WWII above-ground air-raid bunker at ul. Ołbińska 30, the Sybiraków square monument, the riverside Józef Zwierzyniecki Boulevard and Plac Św. Macieja.

Wrocław Nadodrze station (pl. Staszica) was the first station of Wrocław's right-bank Oder railway, opened in 1868 as a temporary station and later expanded in the historicist style, designed by Hermann Grapow. Originally called Rechte-Oder-Ufer-Thorbahnhof, later Breslau Odertor; it received the name Wrocław Nadodrze only after WWII. In the 1980s the building still housed railway offices, a restaurant, a clinic, ticket offices, a railway technical school dormitory and a militia post. Today it is a striking but derelict landmark.

Ulica Bolesława Chrobrego in Nadodrze is a street of 19th-century tenement houses, formerly named Bismarckstrasse in the German era. Many tenements have been restored in recent years. The corner tenement at Chrobrego 2 / Paulińska 22 was renovated and extended between 2004 and 2013; a 1912 photo shows an advertisement for the architecture office of Fritz Engert based on Bismarckstrasse.

# Wrocław Nadodrze: Another World Across the Oder

![Time](/_next/static/media/clock.2bb9e3aa.svg)

3 minutes

[Map](#map)[Places](#places)

Head uptown, north across the wide murky band of the Oder River, and you will encounter a city quarter seemingly in the midst of an identity crisis, where decorative nineteenth-century architecture shares urban space with squats and concrete utilitarian buildings. Crumbling abandoned structures stand side-by-side with brand-spankin'-new playing fields and freshly-painted facades, while a power plant looms over neatly-trimmed greenery. Not grimy and grungy enough to satisfy the odd thrill-seeker, and lacking any true historical landmarks that could help it contest the Old Town, at first glance it might seem that **Nadodrze** doesn't have all that much to offer potential tourists – but dig around a bit and you’ll find a lively art scene, young cultural initiatives, unique workshops, charming cafes, and some of the city's best eats.

![](https://s.inyourpocket.com/img/text/poland/wroclaw/img_5296.jpg) 

Nadodrze straddles the line between shabby and chic, quirky and dodgy - as this odd doorway demonstrates.

This **19th-century artisan district** - [severely damaged during WWII](/poland/wroclaw/articles/festung-breslau:-the-siege-of-1945)and plagued by poverty and alcoholism in the post-war years - has been the **target of a huge urban revitalisation/overhaul project** during the past decade. Once known as a notoriously dangerous and grim neighbourhood, Nadodrze has emerged as a firmly-established **artistic district** drawing creative minds from around the city and spawning new places of interest left and right. With a whole army of enthusiastic, efficient NGOs dedicated to improving every aspect of Nadodrze life - from renovating buildings and courtyards, to breathing life into the cultural landscape, to tackling socioeconomic issues - impressively much has been done here. And it seems the winds of change are blowing ever stronger. Tourists and Wrocław-dwellers are finally starting to appreciate the grand transformation the district has been undergoing and slowly viewing it as **a place to escape the crowded [main square](/poland/wroclaw/venues/market-square)** or to take a break from museum-hopping and ticking off all the obligatory [Wrocław sights](/poland/wroclaw/sightseeing). So don't be shy, dip underneath one of the nondescript archways to any of the spacious courtyards (true feats of 19th-century urban planning) beyond, and see what's been brewing in this off-the-radar area.

## **What to See in Wrocław Nadodrze**

Believe it or not, Nadodrze actually has its own [**info point**](/poland/wroclaw/venues/lokietka-5-infopunkt-nadodrze), just over the river at [**ul. Władysława Łokietka 5/1**](/poland/wroclaw/venues/lokietka-5-infopunkt-nadodrze), which is a great place to gather some intel on the neighbourhood, or connect with its residents.

![](https://s.inyourpocket.com/img/text/poland/wroclaw/nadodrze-air-raid-bunker.jpg) 

WWII air-raid bunker in Nadodrze at ul. Ołbińska 30.

If Nadodrze landmarks are what you're really after, there are a couple things you want to keep an eye out for: **[Wrocław Nadodrze](/poland/wroclaw/venues/dworzec-nadodrze)** - the stunning-yet-derelict 1868 train station designed in the German historicist style by Hermann Grapow; the above-ground WWII-era **air-raid bunker** (located where ul. Św. Wincentego merges into ul. Ołbińska); the monument to Poles exiled to Siberia on **Skwer** **Sybiraków**; and the **Nadodrze power plant** - you won't need a map to find that last one. For the most authentic experience, we would recommend visiting some of the inner-building courtyards, which harbour many of the district's outstanding [**street art murals**](/poland/wroclaw/articles/wherefore-urban-art-thou). Indeed, a mural-safari might be a great way to spend a couple hours – at last count, there were over 30 works of art gracing various walls around the neighbourhood.

![](https://s.inyourpocket.com/img/text/poland/wroclaw/wroclaw-spring-2012-247.jpg) 

A large, whimsical mural just over the river in Nadodrze.

If you're in need of a pleasant stroll or some bench-time, the river-side **Józef Zwierzyniecki Boulevard** is the most charming spot, but the district also has plenty of parks and green squares for you to rest in, the most inviting and expansive of which is bucolic **Plac Św. Macieja** (St. Maciej's Square) at the very heart of the neighbourhood. chunks.content: Nadodrze is an osiedle (settlement/district) in central Wrocław on the right bank of the Oder, formally delineated in 1991. Its area was incorporated into the city between 1768 and 1808 after the demolition of the city fortifications. Population was 22,259 as of 31 Dec 2024. It is a 19th-century artisan district of decorative historicist tenements, severely damaged in WWII and long considered run-down, now known for its art scene, murals, workshops and cafes.

Between 2009 and 2013 Nadodrze underwent a major urban revitalisation programme costing an estimated 150 million PLN (~36 million EUR), aiming to transform an area previously perceived as slums with crumbling tenements into a prestigious, creative district. The strategy favoured murals and artistic installations over demolition; over 30 street-art works decorate walls and courtyards. Landmarks include the 1868 Nadodrze railway station, a WWII above-ground air-raid bunker at ul. Ołbińska 30, the Sybiraków square monument, the riverside Józef Zwierzyniecki Boulevard and Plac Św. Macieja.

Wrocław Nadodrze station (pl. Staszica) was the first station of Wrocław's right-bank Oder railway, opened in 1868 as a temporary station and later expanded in the then-fashional historicist style, designed by Hermann Grapow. Originally called Rechte-Oder-Ufer-Thorbahnhof, later Breslau Odertor; it received the name Wrocław Nadodrze only after WWII. In the 1980s the building still housed railway offices, a restaurant, a clinic, ticket offices, a railway technical school dormitory and a militia post. Today it is a striking but derelict landmark.

Ulica Bolesława Chrobrego in Nadodrze is a street of 19th-century tenement houses (built up around 1895-1905), formerly named Bismarckstrasse in the German era and later ul. Stalina in the communist period. Many tenements have been restored in recent years. The corner tenement at Chrobrego 2 / Paulińska 22 was renovated and extended between 2004 and 2013; a 1912 photo shows an advertisement for the architecture office of Fritz Engert based on Bismarckstrasse.

Plac Św. Macieja (St. Maciej's Square) lies at the heart of Nadodrze and is described as the most inviting and expansive of the district's green squares, a pleasant spot for a rest during a walk through the neighbourhood.
